title: Dry-run: a transaction that looks safe and isn't
intro: About 5 minutes. A money transfer is the classic example because the bug is invisible until two requests race.

steps.title: The naive transfer — two separate statements, no transaction
steps.explain: Without wrapping both statements together, a crash or error between them leaves the debit applied and the credit missing — money has vanished from the system, which is the one thing a ledger must never do.

steps.title: Fix: wrap both statements in one transaction
steps.explain: BEGIN/COMMIT makes the two updates atomic — either both apply or neither does, even across a crash. This alone fixes the vanishing-money bug, but not a subtler one that shows up under concurrency.
steps.saysOutLoud: Atomicity fixes the crash case. It does not fix two transfers racing each other.

steps.title: The race the transaction alone doesn't stop
steps.explain: Two concurrent transfers both reading account A's balance before either writes can both pass a balance check that should have failed one of them — a classic lost-update. Wrapping statements in BEGIN/COMMIT does not by itself prevent two transactions from reading the same stale value.
steps.code:
-- Transaction 1 and Transaction 2, both starting with balance = 100:
-- T1: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id='A';        -- reads 100
-- T2: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id='A';        -- reads 100
-- T1: UPDATE ... SET balance = 100 - 80 WHERE id='A';    -- ok, 80 >= 0
-- T2: UPDATE ... SET balance = 100 - 80 WHERE id='A';    -- also thinks ok!
-- Result: -60, an overdraft that should have been rejected

steps.title: Fix: let the WHERE clause enforce the invariant atomically
steps.explain: Checking the balance in the same statement that updates it removes the read-then-write gap entirely — the database evaluates the condition and the write as one atomic step, so a concurrent transaction can't sneak in between them.
steps.code:
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE id = 'A' AND balance >= 100;

-- check rows affected: 0 means the debit was correctly rejected

steps.title: The composite index has to match the query's leading column
steps.explain: An index on (user_id, created_at) serves 'transactions for this user, ordered by time' as a single range scan. Swap the column order and the same query degrades to scanning every row for a matching created_at, because the index can't be used to narrow by user_id first.
steps.saysOutLoud: Index column order has to match how the query filters, not just which columns it touches.

steps.title: Isolation level is a trade you state, not a default you accept
steps.explain: READ COMMITTED (many databases' default) still allows the lost-update above unless you use the WHERE-clause trick or SERIALIZABLE. Naming the isolation level you're relying on, and why, is what separates 'it happened to work' from an actual guarantee.
steps.code:
-- READ COMMITTED: sees other committed writes, but the race above is still
--   possible unless the WHERE clause carries the check (as fixed above).
-- SERIALIZABLE:    prevents it outright, at the cost of more transaction
--   aborts under contention that the app must be ready to retry.

closing: If they ask why not just lock the row: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE works too and is sometimes clearer to read, but it holds a lock for the transaction's duration — the atomic WHERE-clause update is usually cheaper because there's no separate read step to protect.
